analysis.one_liner: Gives government-funded lawyers to immigrants facing deportation who cannot afford one.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the Senate in August 2026 with nine original sponsors and eight cosponsors, all Democrats or allied independents; referred to the Judiciary Committee, which has taken no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would write a right to a lawyer, paid for by the government, into deportation and immigration detention proceedings for anyone who cannot afford one — with counsel appointed within 24 hours of being taken into custody. It would create an independent Office of Immigration Representation, run like the federal public defender system, with local boards, salaried immigration public defenders, and a roster of private attorneys paid by the hour. Proceedings could not begin until a lawyer is appointed, people would get a copy of their full government immigration file, and the office's funding would be set at a fixed ratio to what the government spends on immigration enforcement and prosecution.
analysis.who_benefits: Immigrants facing deportation, exclusion, bond hearings, or expedited removal who cannot afford a lawyer — including people detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement or Customs and Border Protection. Research and experience with the current system show unrepresented people in immigration court rarely win relief; this bill would guarantee them a lawyer from the moment of detention through any appeal, plus interpreters, investigators, and expert help, and would bar receiving a court-appointed lawyer from counting against them in a public-charge determination.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Immigrants facing deportation who can't afford counsel

how_it_helps.text: Anyone financially unable to obtain a lawyer — a sworn statement of family income at or below 200% of the poverty line qualifies — is entitled to government-paid counsel in every removal, exclusion, deportation, bond, or expedited removal proceeding, from first appearance through the Supreme Court.

For people detained by the Department of Homeland Security or Health and Human Services, the right to counsel attaches the moment they are taken into custody, and a lawyer must be appointed no later than 24 hours later.

Removal proceedings cannot commence until counsel is appointed; the person and their lawyer receive a complete copy of the government's immigration file within 7 days, and proceedings cannot start until at least 10 days after the documents arrive unless waived.

Detained people must get confidential, in-person or remote meetings with their lawyer during the first 12 hours of detention, and any statement made before access to counsel is provided cannot be used against them.
Seeking or receiving appointed counsel may not be treated as evidence that someone is likely to become a 'public charge' for immigration purposes.

The bill creates an independent, nonpartisan Office of Immigration Representation — governed by a board appointed by federal appeals-court chief judges — to run local defender organizations and a compensated private-attorney panel, with pay set to match what government prosecutors earn in the same area.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers fund the new Office of Immigration Representation, its salaried defenders, and hourly panel attorneys — with a statutory funding floor tied to a fixed ratio of what Congress appropriates for ICE, Border Patrol, and DOJ immigration litigation. Enforcement agencies also bear new duties: providing confidential lawyer access within 12 hours of detention, handing over complete files within a week, and halting proceedings where counsel is not provided.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes open-ended appropriations 'such sums as may be necessary' and sets a minimum funding formula tied to enforcement budgets, a large and recurring new federal expense with no cost estimate in the bill text.

Proceedings cannot start until counsel is appointed and cannot begin until at least 10 days after the person receives their full government file, which would slow the pace of the immigration court system; anyone moved between states or detention facilities must be connected to new local counsel.
The bill has been in the Senate Judiciary Committee since the day it was introduced, with no hearing, markup, or vote scheduled as of the last recorded action.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core promise — no one deported without a lawyer if they cannot afford one — is a major due-process protection for a population that currently mostly faces immigration court alone, where unrepresented people rarely prevail. The real costs are money and speed: a large permanent federal legal-aid program and procedures that would make many cases take longer. An honest supporter would also note that eligibility keyed to 200% of the poverty line and an open-ended funding formula raise fairness and budgeting questions of their own. Weighing it, the due-process gain is substantial, but the price tag is real and unevaluated.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in early August 2026 and sent straight to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which has not scheduled any hearing, markup, or vote; with the Congress running into January 2027, the bill is simply waiting.

narrative.text: Senator Adam Schiff introduced the bill on August 6, 2026, joined by eight original cosponsors.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
No further action is recorded: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action.
Its cosponsors are 7 of 45 Senate Democrats plus 1 of 2 Senate independents; no Republican has signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one yet. The bill sits in committee, and the current system — where most people facing deportation have no lawyer — remains in place for now. The status quo, which enforcement agencies and the government's side of immigration court operate under unchanged, is what continues.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet — the bill awaits committee action

sides.party_line_note: All nine original sponsors are Democrats or independents who caucus with them, and none of its eight cosponsors is a Republican [S3]; no Republican has opposed it on the record, but the Republican-led committee and Senate have simply not acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would make lawyers for immigrants a permanent, government-funded line of work: salaried immigration public defender organizations and a paid panel of private attorneys, reimbursed at rates matching government prosecutors. Immigrants gain counsel, and the legal-services field gains a locked-in funding stream.

industries.industry: Immigration enforcement agencies (ICE, CBP, DOJ immigration litigation)
industries.note: The agencies would have to provide confidential lawyer access within 12 hours of detention, surrender complete files within a week, and stop using statements taken before counsel access; proceedings halt where no lawyer is appointed. Their budget, however, becomes the yardstick that sets the defense office's minimum funding.

analysis.trajectory: Bills introduced in August of a two-year Congress with no committee action typically die without a vote when the Congress ends in early January. Unless the Judiciary Committee schedules a hearing or the provisions are attached to a larger must-pass package, this bill is likely to expire at the end of the session and have to be reintroduced next Congress.
